title: “Well-Organised Misunderstanding": The Fine Art of Being Wrong
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick explains how Michelene Chi's 2008 chapter on conceptual change overturned his assumption that student misconceptions are simply gaps in knowledge. Following Chi, he argues that many errors are coherent but incorrect mental models, so students reason logically from wrong premises and absorb corrective facts into the flawed framework rather than abandoning it. He sets out Chi's three levels of error: isolated false beliefs that yield to direct refutation, flawed mental models that need transformation, and ontological category mistakes (heat as a substance, force as a thing) that require a categorical shift. From this he builds a critique of teaching 'critical thinking skills' in isolation, contending that better reasoning applied to a miscategorised concept merely produces more articulate wrong answers. The practical move is to defend explicit and Direct Instruction as diagnostic teaching, where constant checking for understanding and the 'we do' phase surface students' underlying models so they can be confronted and rebuilt. He closes by framing teaching as understanding the logic behind persistent errors well enough to help students reorganise the categories through which they see the world.
points: Chi's phrase 'well-organised misunderstanding' captures the claim that misconceptions are often internally consistent models, not ignorance, which is why stating the correct fact can leave them enriched but still wrong.

Chi distinguishes false beliefs, flawed mental models and ontological category mistakes, and each needs a different instructional response, from simple refutation to dismantling and rebuilding a category.
Even explicit feedback (as in the Law and Ogborne programming study) can produce surface rule changes without shifting the core hypotheses beneath a student's model.
Hendrick argues that critical thinking taught as a generic skill fails because sharpened reasoning operating on a flawed model just makes students better at defending the wrong conclusion.
He reframes 'I do, we do, you do' as gradual revelation of student thinking, arguing explicit instruction especially benefits disadvantaged students who lack the right conceptual frameworks.
quotes: When I first started teaching almost 20 years ago, I used to think that when students gave wrong answers, they simply lacked the correct knowledge, that misconceptions were just gaps to be filled. But then I encountered Michelene Chi's work, and I realised I was wrong about being wrong.

In other words, you can't overwrite a misconception with a fact; you have to confront and replace the flawed model itself. Contradiction is key. For change to happen, students must recognise that what they believed is incompatible with the correct view.
This resonates deeply with my own experience of marking student work. I've seen students make surface-level corrections while maintaining the same fundamental errors across multiple attempts.

In other words, reasoning skill alone doesn’t guarantee accurate reasoning. As Daniel Willingham has pointed out, critical thinking is not a generic set of moves that float free of content. We think critically about something, and the quality of that thinking depends on the accuracy and depth of the knowledge we bring to bear.

If we want students to think critically, we must first make sure they are thinking with the right concepts. That means identifying, surfacing, and, when necessary, dismantling flawed mental models, not just teaching abstract heuristics about argument and evidence. Otherwise, we risk creating highly articulate students who can argue brilliantly… for things that aren’t true.

For example, the "I do, we do, you do" structure isn't just about gradual release of responsibility, it's about gradual revelation of student thinking. During the "we do" phase, teachers can observe student responses, catch misconceptions early, and provide immediate corrective feedback before errors become entrenched. This is conceptual change in real time.

Chi's framework reminds us that behind every persistent error lies a logical system trying to make sense of the world. So I guess our job isn't to dismiss that logic but to understand it well enough to help students build something better.
